chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Yazid ibn Ishaq from Harun ibn Hamzah al-Ghanawi from Hariz from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
Any man who has a dispute over a right with his brother, and calls him to a man from their peers to judge between them, but he refuses except to refer him to these [rulers/judges],

is in the position of those of whom Allah the Exalted said, 'Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you, who desire to take cases in jurisdiction to the Taghut, while they have been commanded to reject them?' [the verse].
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on referring disputes to secular courts instead of religious judges?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) to establish the hierarchy of judicial authority, warning that refusing a designated religious arbitrator in favor of secular or arbitrary powers (*Taghut*) constitutes a spiritual deviation. This principle underscores the Shia emphasis on *Hukm al-Qada* (judicial ruling) within the community, linking the rejection of religious arbitration directly to the Quranic critique of those who seek validation from worldly powers over divine decree. It serves as a foundational text for the legitimacy of the *Ulama* and Imams in resolving disputes, contrasting them with the *Taghut* of the era.
